clue.text: "Realist" novel of London from strangely vegetal penman

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the two words that follow are put in an odd new order

explanation.surface: A London novel said to come from a writer whose style is oddly vegetable-like.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strangely' rearranges VEGETAL PENMAN. The answer is J. B. Priestley's 1930 novel of London office life, often called realist.
explanation.definitionFit: Priestley's novel about a firm in a dingy City street is a realistic portrait of London.

clue.text: A good year for Larkin and Dryden

definitions.meaning: a wonderful twelve months, in Latin
both poets wrote a poem with this Latin title

explanation.surface: A fine vintage year enjoyed by two poets.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means a year of wonders; Dryden's 1667 poem and Larkin's 1967 poem share the title.

clue.text: Friend of Chaucer from Welsh peninsula

definitions.meaning: the medieval poet John of that surname, whom Chaucer called moral
the promontory west of Swansea in South Wales

explanation.surface: A companion of Chaucer who hailed from Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gower was Chaucer's contemporary and friend; the Gower Peninsula juts out from South Wales.

clue.text: Henry, traitor to Henry

parts.note: a nobleman named Henry who plots against King Henry in Shakespeare's history play about Agincourt

explanation.surface: One Henry betrays another.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Henry V, Henry, Lord Scroop of Masham conspires against the king and is executed.

clue.text: Argonaut, producing a list of characters (American)

parts.note: the cast of a play is its list of characters

explanation.surface: One of Jason's crew writes the dramatis personae for a US production.
explanation.definitionFit: Acastus, son of Pelias, sailed with Jason on the Argo in Greek myth.

clue.text: Enduring, like Manning's priesthood

definitions.meaning: lasting for ever
Cardinal Manning wrote a book on the priesthood with this adjective in its title

explanation.surface: A lasting quality, compared with a cardinal's view of holy orders.
explanation.definitionFit: Something everlasting endures; Henry Edward Manning published The Eternal Priesthood in 1883.

clue.text: Heroic work must be in the picture

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the run of words the picture

explanation.surface: A grand saga has to feature in the film.
explanation.definitionFit: An epic is a long poem or story recounting heroic deeds.

clue.text: Strangely vile trash of D' Avenant, anticipating Sheridan

indicators.note: strangely says the letters of the two words that follow are jumbled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Restoration dramatist's play, oddly dismissed as rubbish, came before Sheridan's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strangely' rearranges VILE TRASH. Davenant's 1664 play of this title preceded Sheridan's famous 1775 comedy with the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both Sir William Davenant and, a century later, Richard Brinsley Sheridan wrote plays called The Rivals.

clue.text: Matching Shavian piece

definitions.meaning: being paired off in wedlock
a play by George Bernard Shaw

explanation.surface: A Shaw play about things that go together.
explanation.definitionFit: Two people being matched are entering wedlock; Shaw's 1908 comedy debates the institution of marriage.

clue.text: "Or did the letters work upon his blood, / And this fault?" (Othello)

definitions.text: "Or did the letters work upon his blood, / And this fault?" (Othello)

parts.words: "Or did the letters work upon his blood, / And this fault?" (Othello)
parts.note: a quotation from Shakespeare's tragedy with a two-word phrase missing before the words this fault

explanation.surface: A line from Othello with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Lodovico asks whether letters have so worked on Othello's blood as to bring a new fault into being; the missing words fill the gap in the second line.
explanation.definitionFit: To make afresh is the sense of the missing verb phrase in Lodovico's speech.

clue.text: Scottish princess as Greek goddess in Johnson tragedy? ()

definitions.meaning: the heroine of George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin; MacDonald was Scottish
the deity personifying peace
Samuel Johnson's only play, staged by Garrick in 1749

explanation.surface: A princess from Scotland plays a Greek deity in Dr Johnson's drama.
explanation.definitionFit: MacDonald's princess, the Greek goddess of peace and Johnson's Byzantine tragedy all bear the name Irene.

clue.text: Berkeley explores the paranormal in palindrome

indicators.note: says the word reads the same forwards and backwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A philosopher looks into the supernatural, writing in a way that reads both ways.
explanation.walkthrough: Bishop Berkeley's late work Siris moves from the virtues of tar-water to mystical speculation; its title is a palindrome.
explanation.definitionFit: Siris (1744) is George Berkeley's treatise that strays from medicine into metaphysics and the occult.

clue.text: Next, Durrell's work starts to upset neat concepts

indicators.note: starts says to take the opening letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: Next comes a Durrell novel that sets out to overturn tidy ideas.
explanation.walkthrough: The title is Latin for 'then', hence 'Next'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence Durrell's 1968 novel bears a Latin title meaning then or thereupon, and it was followed by Nunquam.

clue.text: Disorder of trio out of tune

indicators.note: out of tune suggests the letters are jangled out of their proper order

explanation.surface: A musical trio plays badly off-key.
explanation.definitionFit: A riot is a violent public disturbance, a breakdown of order.

clue.text: Sign presaging women in love?

parts.note: a token of God's covenant after the Flood, and also the D. H. Lawrence novel that came before his Women in Love

explanation.surface: An omen that women are about to fall in love.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's 1915 novel preceded Women in Love, and the arc in the sky was Noah's sign of promise.

clue.text: Ernst is mistaken, making late additions

indicators.note: mistaken means the letters of the preceding two words are in the wrong order

explanation.surface: The painter Ernst makes errors and has to add things at the last minute.
explanation.definitionFit: Inserts are extra pages or passages added into a text, often late in production.

clue.text: Lively story with well-woven thread?

definitions.meaning: a novel by Penelope Lively (1998)
silk spun neatly by an arachnid

explanation.surface: A vivid tale with a skilfully interwoven plot.
explanation.definitionFit: Penelope Lively's 1998 novel has this title, and a cobweb is thread finely woven.

clue.text: Early Hogarth Press worker not of the cloth, say

indicators.note: say signals that the word is to be heard rather than spelt

parts.note: a layman is someone who is not a member of the clergy

explanation.surface: An early employee of the Woolfs' press who was not a clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: John Lehmann worked at the Hogarth Press, run by Leonard and Virginia Woolf, from 1931.
explanation.definitionFit: John Lehmann joined Leonard and Virginia Woolf's publishing house as manager in its early years.

clue.text: Piece of publicity I come to with an attitude — possibly Falstaffian

parts.note: a pose is a stance or attitude

explanation.surface: An advert in which I strike a pose, perhaps as Shakespeare's fat knight.
explanation.definitionFit: Adipose means fatty, and Falstaff is Shakespeare's famously corpulent knight.

clue.text: Clue "ego", perhaps for pastoral poem

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters given could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: A crossword hint to the word ego, offered for a country poem.
explanation.definitionFit: An eclogue is a short poem of shepherds' dialogue, like Virgil's Eclogues.

clue.text: "Mr Badman died like a lamb, or… like a child" (Bunyan)

definitions.text: "Mr Badman died like a lamb, or… like a child" (Bunyan)

parts.words: "Mr Badman died like a lamb, or… like a child" (Bunyan)
parts.note: a quotation from Bunyan with one adjective missing before the word child

explanation.surface: A line from Bunyan with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Bunyan's The Life and Death of Mr Badman says he died 'like a lamb, or, as men call it, like a chrisom child, quietly and without fear'.
explanation.definitionFit: A chrisom child was an infant who died in its christening robe, within a month of baptism.

clue.text: Clique receiving contributions from Lawrence, Eliot, Huxley and Edith Sitwell

definitions.meaning: a small exclusive circle

definitions.text: receiving contributions from Lawrence, Eliot, Huxley and Edith Sitwell
definitions.meaning: a little magazine of 1919 to 1921 that printed these writers

explanation.surface: An in-group of modernist writers sends in pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A close circle of friends is a set, and Coterie was a short-lived literary journal publishing modernists.

clue.text: Composer of Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau

definitions.text: Composer of Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau

parts.words: Composer of Emerson, Hawthorne, the Alcotts and Thoreau
parts.note: the four movements of the Concord Sonata are named after New England writers

explanation.surface: A musician who set the Concord writers to music.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Ives's Piano Sonata No. 2, Concord, Mass., 1840-60, has movements titled after those four.

clue.text: Conspire in novel construction

definitions.meaning: scheme together secretly
the storyline of a work of fiction

explanation.surface: Scheming within the structure of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Conspirators scheme together, and the storyline is the structure a novelist builds.

clue.text: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden

definitions.text: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden

parts.words: Sort of play by Beatrice Harraden
parts.note: a prefix that joins the word play to make the title of a Harraden novel of 1908

explanation.surface: A kind of drama written by a novelist of the 1890s.
explanation.definitionFit: Harraden's novel Interplay takes its title from this prefix put before play.

clue.text: Revolting Southey protagonist ()

parts.note: the leader of the Peasants' Revolt, hero of Southey's youthful verse drama

explanation.surface: A repulsive hero created by Southey.
explanation.definitionFit: Southey's Wat Tyler dramatises the leader of the 1381 rising against the poll tax.

clue.text: Apparent subject of Nina Bawden

parts.note: the girl whose name precedes Apparent in the title of a Bawden novel of 1972

explanation.surface: What Nina Bawden seems to be writing about.
explanation.definitionFit: Nina Bawden's novel Anna Apparent centres on its heroine Anna.

clue.text: Historical novelist who showed her hand (a hard one to beat) ()

definitions.text: Historical novelist who showed her hand (a hard one to beat)

parts.words: Historical novelist who showed her hand (a hard one to beat)
parts.note: the author of the novel Royal Flush, named after the top poker hand

explanation.surface: A writer of period fiction laid down her cards, an unbeatable set.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Irwin wrote historical novels, including Royal Flush (1932), titled after poker's best hand.

clue.text: M.E. Braddon's verse takes the biscuit

definitions.meaning: Mary Elizabeth Braddon published a volume of poems named after the Italian patriot
a currant biscuit named after the same Italian

explanation.surface: Braddon's poetry wins the prize.
explanation.definitionFit: Braddon's Garibaldi and Other Poems appeared in 1861; the currant-filled biscuit honours the same general.

clue.text: Miranda's sweet sentiment, somewhat soured by Huxley

definitions.meaning: her exclamation of wonder on seeing people in The Tempest
Aldous Huxley borrowed the phrase for his dystopian novel

explanation.surface: Miranda's innocent delight turned sour by a later writer.
explanation.definitionFit: Miranda cries 'O brave new world' in The Tempest; Huxley used it ironically for his 1932 dystopia.
